title: Tale of the Kazi and the Bhang-Eater (简体中文)
summary: In Damascus lived an idle dreamer named Bakr, who spent his days consuming intoxicating herbal pastes and dreaming extravagant daydreams ... [ZH]
keywords: tale of the kazi and the bhang-eater
full_text:
In Damascus lived an idle dreamer named Bakr, who spent his days consuming intoxicating herbal pastes and dreaming extravagant daydreams in sunny courtyards instead of working.

One sunny afternoon, under the influence of his delusions, Bakr imagined he was the Grand Emperor of China, seated upon a throne of solid sapphire, distributing sacks of emeralds to kneeling ambassadors.
He began commanding imaginary armies at the top of his voice: 'Bring forth the golden elephants! Let the dancing peacocks assemble!'

A crowd gathered, laughing at his antics, until the municipal guards arrested him for disturbing the peace and hauled him before the austere City Kazi.

The Kazi glared at Bakr and demanded: 'Why dost thou cause public disorder and shout senseless commands in the marketplace?'

Bakr, still half-entangled in his reverie, blinked and replied:
'Your Honor, in my dream I was an all-powerful emperor who could grant wishes and heal poverty with a wave of my hand. If a man may be a glorious king in his sleep for free, why should he wake up to be a hungry porter in Damascus?'

The Kazi stroked his beard, saw through the poor man's delusion, and ordered:
'Place this Emperor of China in a cool bath, feed him warm chicken broth with lime juice, and bring him back when his head is clear.'

The next morning, with the fog of herbs gone, Bakr returned to court shivering in an ordinary woolen tunic.
The Kazi asked: 'Where are thy sapphire thrones and golden elephants today, O Emperor?'
Bakr hung his head: 'They vanished into thin air, your Honor, leaving me with a pounding headache and an empty stomach.'

The Kazi smiled gently:
'Dreaming of glory while neglecting the work before thee is like pouring perfume into a broken jug. Imaginary riches cannot buy a loaf of bread, and a clouded mind loses the true sweetness of life. Take this silver coin, buy a basket and pruning shears, and earn thy bread in the fig orchards. For an honest copper earned by the sweat of thy brow is worth ten thousand imaginary empires.'

Bakr took the counsel to heart, threw away his intoxicating herbs, and became an industrious gardener, enjoying the clear sunshine of reality.
moral: Illusions born of indolence vanish like smoke; genuine peace is found in clear minds and honest reality. [ZH]
